Key Takeaways
Yarn count defines fineness through direct systems such as Tex and Denier, and indirect systems such as Ne, Nw, and Nm, giving the base for twist, tenacity, fabric weight, cover, and handle.
Twist, strength, and elongation show how fibres hold together and withstand processing stresses, with testing methods ranging from twist testers to single-end, lea, and tensile tests.

Yarn quality shapes every later stage of textile production. It affects how a yarn runs in winding, warping, weaving, and knitting. It also affects how the finished fabric looks and performs. For this reason, spinning mills and testing laboratories measure a set of basic yarn properties as a routine part of quality control.

This article discusses six of these properties: yarn count, twist, strength, elongation, uniformity, and hairiness. For each property, it covers the definition, the units of measurement, the principles of testing, and the practical significance. It closes with a note on how these properties relate to one another.

Yarn Count Systems

Yarn count expresses the fineness of a yarn. Yarn diameter is difficult to measure because yarn is soft and compressible. Count is therefore defined as a relationship between the length and the weight of a yarn.

Yarn count or Linear density of yarn is expressed in two ways: direct and indirect system.

A. Direct Count System

In the direct system, length is constant and weight is variable. Linear density is expressed directly, as mass per unit length.

The higher the count, the coarser the yarn.

There are two direct systems: Tex and Denier.

1. Tex System: The Tex number is the weight in grams of 1,000 metres of the material.

Formula: Tex = (Weight in grams ÷ Length in metres) × 1000

2. Denier System: Denier is the weight in grams of 9,000 metres of the material.

Formula: Denier = (Weight in grams ÷ Length in metres) × 9000

B. Indirect Count System

In the indirect system, weight is constant and length is variable. Count is expressed indirectly, as length per unit mass.

The higher the count, the finer the yarn.

There are three indirect systems: Cotton (English) Count (Ne), Worsted Count (Nw), and Metric Count (Nm).

English Count (Cotton Count): English Count is the number of hanks, each 840 yards long, that weigh one pound.

Formula: English Count (Ne) = (Length in yards ÷ Weight in pounds) ÷ 840

A longer length in the same weight means a finer yarn.

Worsted Count: Worsted Count is the number of hanks, each 560 yards long that weigh one pound.

Formula: Worsted Count = (Length in yards ÷ Weight in pounds) ÷ 560

Metric Count: Metric Count is the number of kilometre lengths of yarn that weigh one kilogram.

Formula: Metric Count (Nm) = Length in metres ÷ Weight in grams

Conversions

The following relationships are used to convert between systems:

Tex = 590.5 / Ne
Denier = 9 × Tex
Nm = 1000 / Tex
Ne = 0.5905 × Nm

Methods of Testing

Count is usually found by measuring a known length of yarn and weighing it. For cotton, a lea of 120 yards is wound on a wrap reel and weighed. If the lea is weighed in grains, the English count is found as follows:

Formula: Ne = 1000 / weight of lea (grains)

This follows from the definition, since one pound equals 7,000 grains. Balances such as the quadrant balance and the Knowles balance give the count directly.

The Beesley balance is useful when only short lengths of yarn are available, such as yarn taken from a fabric.

Significance

Count is the starting point for most other yarn tests. The twist multiplier, tenacity, and Count Strength Product all use count in their calculation. Count also decides fabric weight, cover, and handle.

Twist

Twist is the number of turns inserted per unit length of yarn. It binds the fibres together and gives the yarn its coherence and strength.

Units and Direction

Twist is expressed in turns per inch (TPI) or turns per metre (TPM). Its direction is described as S or Z. The letter used is the one whose middle stroke matches the slope of the fibres when the yarn is held vertically.

Twist Multiplier

Twist is linked to yarn count through the twist multiplier (TM). In the English cotton count system:

Formula: TM = TPI / vNe

A higher twist multiplier gives a harder and stronger yarn, but only up to a limit.

Methods of Testing

Two methods are commonly used. Both use a twist tester fitted with a pre-tension weight and a revolution counter.

A. Direct Counting Method: The yarn is untwisted until the fibres or plies lie parallel, and the turns are counted. This method suits plied yarns and filament yarns, where the components can be separated clearly.

B. Untwist–Retwist Method: This method suits single spun yarns, where the fibres cannot be made fully parallel. As the yarn is untwisted, it extends. It is then twisted in the opposite direction until it returns to its original length. The total number of turns is divided by two to give the twist.

Significance

Yarn strength rises with twist up to an optimum level. Beyond this level, strength falls, because the fibres become too oblique to the yarn axis. Twist also affects the handle, lustre, bulk, and dye uptake of a yarn.

Strength

Yarn strength is the force needed to break the yarn.

Measures

Strength can be expressed in several ways.

•   Breaking force is measured in centinewtons (cN) or grams-force.

•   Tenacity is breaking force divided by linear density, expressed in cN/tex. It allows yarns of different counts to be compared fairly.

•   RKM (breaking length) is the length of yarn, in kilometres, whose own weight equals its breaking force.

•   Count Strength Product (CSP) is lea strength in pounds multiplied by the English count. It is widely used in Indian spinning mills.

Methods of Testing

In the single-end test, one strand is broken at a time. Modern single-end testers work on the constant rate of extension principle. In the lea test, a skein of 120 yards, made of 80 wraps on a 1.5-yard wrap reel, is broken as a whole.

Principles of Tensile Testers

Tensile testers work on one of three principles. Constant rate of extension (CRE) testers stretch the specimen at a steady rate; examples include the Instron and the Uster Tensorapid. Constant rate of loading (CRL) testers increase the load at a steady rate. Constant rate of traverse (CRT) testers move one jaw at a steady rate and are found in older pendulum-lever machines.

Significance

Strength determines whether a yarn can withstand the stresses of winding, warping, sizing, weaving, and knitting without frequent breaks.

Elongation

Elongation is the increase in length of a yarn at the point of break. It is expressed as a percentage of the original test length:

Formula: Elongation (per cent) = (extension at break / initial length) × 100

Method of Testing

Elongation is recorded together with strength, on the same tensile tester and in the same test. The tester also produces a load–elongation curve. The area under this curve gives the work of rupture, which reflects the toughness of the yarn.

Significance

Adequate elongation helps a yarn absorb sudden loads during weaving and knitting. Yarn with low elongation causes more end breaks and loom stoppages.

Uniformity (Evenness)

Uniformity, or evenness, is the consistency of mass per unit length along a yarn.

Measures

U per cent is the mean deviation of mass from the average.

CV per cent is the coefficient of variation of mass.

Imperfections are counted per kilometre, usually as a total called the imperfection index (IPI). They include thin places (-50 per cent), thick places (+50 per cent), and neps (+200 per cent for ring-spun yarn).

Principle of Testing

The capacitance method is the most widely used, for example in the Uster Tester. The yarn passes between two capacitor plates. Any change in yarn mass changes the capacitance, and this change is recorded as an evenness signal. Some modern testers also use optical sensors to measure yarn diameter.

Supporting Tools

A spectrogram identifies periodic faults, such as those caused by eccentric drafting rollers. Uster Statistics serve as benchmarks for comparing a mill's yarn with world production. The seriplane or blackboard appearance test is a visual method. Yarn is wound on a black board and graded against standard photographs.

Significance

Uneven yarn contains weak places, which lead to end breaks. It also produces visible fabric faults, such as streaks, barré, and cloudiness.

Hairiness

Hairiness refers to the fibre ends and loops that protrude from the body of a yarn.

Measures

The Uster H value is the total length, in centimetres, of protruding fibres per centimetre of yarn. It has no unit.

The Zweigle S3 value is the number of hairs 3 mm or longer per 100 metres of yarn.

Principle of Testing

Most hairiness testers are optical. A light beam falls on the moving yarn. The protruding fibres scatter or interrupt the light, and photo detectors count or measure them. The Shirley hairiness meter counts hairs that extend beyond a set distance from the yarn core.

Factors Affecting Hairiness

Hairiness depends on fibre length, the spinning system, the twist level, spindle speed, and the condition of the traveller. Compact-spun yarn has lower hairiness than conventional ring-spun yarn. Higher twist generally reduces hairiness.

Significance

High hairiness causes pilling, fluff generation, and problems in sizing. It also reduces the clarity of the fabric surface. Some hairiness is desirable, however, where a soft handle is needed.

These six properties do not act alone. Count forms the basis for the twist multiplier and for strength measures such as fineness, tenacity, and CSP. Twist gives structure and lowers hairiness. Poor evenness produces thin places, which become weak points and reduce both strength and elongation. Strength and elongation show how the yarn handles stress. Uniformity and hairiness show how consistent and clean the yarn is. Together, they form the core of yarn quality control.

Yarn quality should therefore be judged on the full set of properties. A yarn that performs well on one property may still fail in use if it performs poorly on another.

Conclusion

These six properties do not act alone. Count forms the basis for the twist multiplier and for strength measures such as fineness, tenacity and CSP. Twist gives structure and lowers hairiness.

Poor evenness produces thin places, which become weak points and reduce both strength and elongation. Strength and elongation show how the yarn handles stress. Uniformity and hairiness show how consistent and clean the yarn is.

Together, they form the core of yarn quality control. Yarn quality should therefore be judged on the full set of properties. A yarn that performs well on one property may still fail in use if it performs poorly on another.
